# Military engineering (roads, bridges, pioneers) (`military_engineering_roads_bridges`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/military.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Warfare, security & deterrence (`military`)
- Deps: helped by surveying_triangulation, paved_roads_macadam, arch_bridge_truss, block_and_tackle, hydraulic_cement
- Core idea: An army moves only as fast as its roads and river crossings allow, so a corps of trained builders with tools belongs to it. Core techniques: an all-weather road on a drained, cambered bed of graded stone; a bridge of boats anchored upstream, decked with planks; a trestle bridge on piles driven by a drop weight from a raft, braced against the current. Caesar bridged the Rhine, some 400 m wide, in ten days. Roads and bridges built for the army then serve trade and government.
- Pitfalls:
  - A road without drainage is destroyed by one wet season; the ditches and the camber matter more than the paving
  - Pile bridges without upstream fenders are broken by floating timber, which the enemy will send down
  - Roman roads were built for marching men and pack animals; their gradients are often too steep for heavy wagons
  - A bridge is a bottleneck and a hostage; it must be guarded at both ends
- History: mesopotamia: c. 500 BC – Persian Royal Road from Susa to Sardis with relay stations; greece: 480 BC – Xerxes' two boat bridges over the Hellespont (Herodotus VII.36); rome: 312 BC – Via Appia; 55 BC – Caesar's Rhine bridge; AD 105 – Apollodorus' bridge over the Danube for Trajan; china: c. 212 BC – Qin 'straight road' to the northern frontier; 214 BC – Lingqu canal built to supply an army; americas: 15th c. – Inca road system of some 40,000 km with rope suspension bridges; islamic: 1566 – Suleiman's timber bridge of about 8 km across the Drava marshes at Osijek, used again by the army marching on Vienna in 1683; europe: 1690s – Vauban forms a corps of engineers in France; 1748 – engineering school at Mézières
- Read:
  - Caesar, De bello Gallico IV.17–18
  - J. G. Landels, Engineering in the Ancient World (1978)
  - John Hyslop, The Inka Road System (1984)
